533.title: Feed my sheep (John 21:15–25)
533.hook: three questions for Peter, and a closing line: the world could not hold all the books
533.tomorrow: To the ends of the earth
533.howItsDone: Catholics hear John 21 at Mass in the Easter season, and the Church reads Jesus's charge to Peter as part of the foundation of the papacy; feeding the hungry is one of the works of mercy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, breathed: the locked room, and receive ye the Holy Ghost. Your line was peace be to you.

Watch the fires in the last chapters of John. The night Jesus was arrested, Peter stood warming his hands at a charcoal fire in the high priest's courtyard and said three times, I don't know him. Now it's dawn on the shore of the Sea of Galilee. The disciples have been fishing all night. And on the beach, Jesus has made breakfast, fish and bread, cooking over a charcoal fire. John uses the same word, charcoal fire, for both. Peter can hardly miss it.
screen: `A CHARCOAL FIRE, THAT NIGHT.` → `I DON'T KNOW HIM, THREE TIMES.` → `ANOTHER CHARCOAL FIRE, AT DAWN.`

segments.voice: After they've eaten, Jesus turns to Peter. Simon son of John, lovest thou me more than these? Yes, Lord, you know I love you. Feed my lambs. Again: lovest thou me? Yes, Lord. Tend my sheep. And a third time. John says Peter was grieved, because he asked the third time. Three denials, three questions. Peter answers, in the Douay-Rheims: "Lord, thou knowest all things: thou knowest that I love thee." And Jesus says: "Feed my sheep." Jesus doesn't make Peter explain the denials or promise never to fail again. He asks one question, about love, and then hands him work. Each yes becomes a job. In Greek, Jesus uses two different verbs for love, and Peter answers with one of them; scholars still debate how much weight to give that. What isn't debated is the pattern: the man who failed three times is restored three times, by the same fire. Catholics see here Peter given the care of the whole flock, part of the foundation of the Pope's office as the shepherd of the Church. Then John ends his Gospel with a shrug of wonder. Jesus did many other things, he says, and if they were all written down, he supposes the world itself couldn't contain the books. That closes six weeks in John: the Word made flesh, water into wine, Nicodemus at night, the woman at the well, the bread of life, golden lampstands, the good shepherd, Lazarus, the towel, the vine, the cross, and Mary in the garden. Tomorrow, the story keeps going in a second book.

segments.voice: Picture a table, a kitchen counter, a bag of groceries, and ask who in your life could use a meal: a neighbor, a coworker eating lunch alone, someone grieving, a kid, a stranger outside the store. Let one person come clearly to mind, and what you could give them. If you pray, hold Peter's answer, Lord, thou knowest that I love thee, and let the meal be how you say it; if you don't, just hold the person.

534.title: To the ends of the earth (Acts 1:6–8)
534.hook: you shall receive power and be witnesses
534.howItsDone: Catholics hear Acts 1:1–11 on the Solemnity of the Ascension, forty days after Easter (moved to the following Sunday in many places), and Acts is read at weekday and Sunday Masses through the Easter season.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the end of John: three questions on the beach by a charcoal fire. Your line was each yes becomes a job.

Some stories get a sequel. Luke's does. His Gospel finishes with Jesus blessing the disciples and being carried up into heaven. Then he writes a second volume, addressed to the same reader, someone called Theophilus, and opens it by saying, in my first book I told you what Jesus began to do and to teach. Began. Everything so far was the beginning. This is that second book, the Acts of the Apostles. It opens on a hill outside Jerusalem, with the disciples asking the wrong question.
screen: `A SEQUEL, PROMISED.` → `WHAT JESUS BEGAN TO DO.` → `THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES.`

segments.voice: For forty days after the resurrection, Luke says, Jesus has been appearing to them and speaking about the kingdom of God. Now they ask: Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel? It's an understandable question. They want to know when, and they want it to look like what they expected. Jesus doesn't argue. The times, he says, aren't theirs to know. Then he gives them something else, in the Douay-Rheims: "But you shall receive the power of the Holy Ghost coming upon you, and you shall be witnesses unto me in Jerusalem, and in all Judea, and Samaria, and even to the uttermost part of the earth." Then he's lifted up and a cloud takes him out of their sight. That one sentence is a map of the whole book. Acts starts in Jerusalem, moves out into Judea and Samaria, and ends with Paul preaching in Rome, the empire's capital. The word to hold is witness. In Greek it's martys. A witness, in a courtroom, is someone who says what they saw. Not an expert, not a salesman, just someone who was there. In time, Christians used the same word for those who died rather than deny what they'd seen: martyr. The Catechism calls martyrdom the supreme witness. But here Jesus doesn't tell them to die. He tells them who they'll be: people whose lives tell what they've seen. Not you shall do witnessing, but you shall be witnesses. It's a description, not a task list.

segments.voice: Picture yourself from the outside, the way a coworker or a neighbor or a kid sees you on an ordinary day, and ask what they'd say you care about just from watching: not from what you say, but from what you do. No judging, just noticing. If you pray, hold the line, you shall be witnesses unto me; if you don't, just hold the picture.

535.title: Matthias (Acts 1:15–26)
535.hook: they pray, cast lots, and the twelfth place is filled
535.howItsDone: Catholics keep a feast of Saint Matthias, Apostle, and the Church often begins important choices, like a papal conclave, with a Mass asking the Holy Spirit's guidance.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the start of Acts, and the word witness. Your line was you shall be witnesses.

Every team photo with an empty spot has a story. A chair left empty at the table, a name missing from the roster. Someone has to decide whether to fill it, and how. After the Ascension the disciples go back to an upper room in Jerusalem and pray together, about a hundred and twenty of them, Luke says, with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus. There were twelve apostles. Now there are eleven. And Peter, only weeks after his own worst failure, stands up to deal with the empty chair.
screen: `AN EMPTY CHAIR.` → `A HUNDRED AND TWENTY IN PRAYER.` → `TWELVE, NOW ELEVEN.`

segments.voice: Peter speaks about Judas plainly and without gloating: he was numbered with us and had a share in this ministry. Then he gives the qualifications for the empty place. It has to be someone who was with them the whole time, from John's baptism to the day Jesus was taken up, someone who can be a witness with them of the resurrection. Yesterday's word, witness, as the job description. Two men fit: Joseph called Barsabas, also known as Justus, and Matthias. Both, we're told, were there from the start, and Acts tells us nothing more about either one. Then they do two things, in this order. First they pray, saying: Lord, you who know the hearts of all, show which of these two you have chosen. Then they cast lots, something like drawing straws. In the Douay-Rheims: "And they gave them lots, and the lot fell upon Matthias, and he was numbered with the eleven apostles." Casting lots was an old way in Israel of leaving a decision to God; Proverbs says the lot is cast, but the decision is the Lord's. Some readers notice that once the Spirit comes at Pentecost, Acts shows the apostles deciding in other ways, by prayer, discussion and the Spirit's lead. What stays is the order: they prayed first. And Matthias, chosen by a falling lot, is honored by the Church as an apostle. Faithful from the beginning, and Acts never names him again.

536.title: Peter's first sermon (Acts 2:14–41)
536.hook: the man who denied him now preaches, and three thousand are baptized
536.tomorrow: Silver and gold I have none
536.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate Pentecost at the close of the Easter season, reading Acts 2 at Mass, and the Church often calls the day its birthday; adults are often received into the Church at Easter after a period of preparation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Matthias, chosen for the empty place. Your line was they prayed first.

Not long ago, a servant girl in a courtyard asked Peter a simple question, aren't you one of his? And he said he wasn't. Now it's the feast of Pentecost, and Jerusalem is full of devout pilgrims, Luke says, from every nation under heaven. The disciples have just poured out of a house, filled with the Holy Spirit, speaking in languages they never learned, and a crowd has gathered to stare. Some people laugh: they're drunk. And the man who stands up to answer them is Peter.
screen: `A SERVANT GIRL'S QUESTION.` → `PENTECOST, THE CITY PACKED.` → `PETER STANDS UP.`

segments.voice: His opening line is almost a joke. These men aren't drunk, as you suppose; it's only the third hour of the day, nine in the morning. Then he gets serious. He quotes the prophet Joel: in the last days, God says, I will pour out my spirit on all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, young men shall see visions, old men shall dream dreams. This, Peter says, is that. He tells them about Jesus of Nazareth, his miracles, his death, and that God raised him up, and we are all witnesses. There's that word witness again. He quotes the psalms of David, and ends on the claim that God has made this crucified Jesus both Lord and Christ. Luke says the listeners were cut to the heart. They ask, what shall we do? And Peter answers, in the Douay-Rheims: "Do penance, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ, for the remission of your sins: and you shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost." Do penance follows the Latin. The Greek word, metanoēsate, means change your mind, turn around, a whole new direction. That day, Luke says, about three thousand were added. And consider who's speaking. Not a polished speaker. A fisherman who, only weeks earlier, couldn't stand up to a servant girl. That courage didn't come from practice. Acts is clear about where it came from: the Spirit poured out that morning. The coward preached. And Catholics often call that feast the Church's birthday.

If you pray, ask the Holy Spirit for the courage Peter was given; if you don't, simply rehearse the sentence.

537.title: Silver and gold I have none (Acts 3:1–10)
537.hook: but what I have, I give thee: rise and walk
537.howItsDone: Catholics are taught the corporal and spiritual works of mercy, giving not only money but time, care, counsel and prayer to people in need.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Peter's first sermon at Pentecost. Your line was the coward preached.

Anyone who drives knows the little calculation at a red light when someone with a cardboard sign walks between the cars. Do I have cash? Is the light about to change? Do I look, or keep my eyes on the dashboard? Usually the eyes win. Looking is the hard part. Afternoon in Jerusalem, three o'clock, the hour of prayer. Peter and John are walking up to the temple. At one of the gates, a man who has never walked in his life is being set down, the way he is every day, to ask for money.
screen: `THE RED-LIGHT CALCULATION.` → `THREE O'CLOCK, THE HOUR OF PRAYER.` → `A MAN AT THE GATE.`

segments.voice: Luke says he was lame from his mother's womb, carried every day to the gate of the temple called Beautiful, to beg from people going in. He sees Peter and John and asks for alms, the way he asks everyone. Then something unusual happens. Peter, with John, fixes his eyes on him and says, look at us. The man looks up, expecting a coin. And Peter says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Silver and gold I have none; but what I have, I give thee: In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, arise, and walk." Peter takes him by the right hand and lifts him up, and the man's feet and ankles grow strong. He jumps up, stands, walks, and goes into the temple with them, walking and leaping and praising God. Everyone recognizes him: the one from the gate. Notice the order. First, eye contact: look at us. Before anything is given, the man is seen. Then an honest no: I don't have money. Then what Peter does have, which isn't his own: the name of Jesus. Peter's not pretending to be richer than he is, or poorer either. There's a story people tell about Thomas Aquinas visiting the pope while gold was being counted. The pope said, the Church can no longer say silver and gold I have none. And Thomas answered, no, and neither can she say, rise and walk. Nobody can confirm it happened. But it's stuck around for centuries because it names the temptation in today's line.

538.title: We cannot but speak (Acts 4:13–20)
538.hook: ordinary uneducated men astonish the council
538.howItsDone: Catholics read the Acts of the Apostles at Mass through the Easter season, and the Church keeps a feast for Catherine of Siena, a Doctor of the Church with little formal schooling.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the man at the Beautiful gate: silver and gold I have none. Your line was what I have I give.

A diploma on the wall tells you where someone studied. It can't tell you what they've seen. After the healing at the gate, Peter and John spent the night in custody. In the morning they're brought before the council: rulers, elders and scribes, men trained in the law of Moses. Facing them, two fishermen from Galilee. And next to the fishermen, on his own two feet, stands the man who used to beg at the gate. The council has a question for them.
screen: `A DIPLOMA ON THE WALL.` → `A NIGHT IN CUSTODY.` → `THE HEALED MAN STANDS WITH THEM.`

segments.voice: The council asks, by what power, by what name, have you done this? Peter answers: by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth. Then Luke describes the council's reaction. They saw the boldness of Peter and John, realized they were unlettered, ordinary men, and were amazed, and they recognized that these two had been with Jesus. Two Greek words are worth knowing. Agrammatoi: unlettered, not trained in the schools of the law. And idiōtai: ordinary people, private persons, not officials. English later got the word idiot from it, but here it just means laymen. The Douay calls their courage constancy. The Greek is parrēsia, freedom of speech, the boldness to say everything plainly. The council can't say much back, Luke notes, because the healed man is standing right there. So they order the two to stop speaking or teaching in the name of Jesus at all. Peter and John answer: whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, you judge. And then, in the Douay-Rheims: "For we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard." It's not stubbornness, and it isn't a debating point. They simply can't un-see what they saw. It's the word from four days ago, witness, under pressure. And the reason given for their boldness isn't schooling. It's that they had been with Jesus. Catholics see the same pattern in some saints with little schooling. Catherine of Siena, tradition says, learned to write only late in life, and the Church later named her a Doctor of the Church.
screen: `BY WHAT NAME?` · `UNLETTERED, ORDINARY MEN.` · `THEY HAD BEEN WITH JESUS.` · `WHAT WE HAVE SEEN AND HEARD.` · then, large: `WE CANNOT BUT SPEAK.`

segments.voice: Let your mind go back to one thing you've witnessed yourself and can't un-see: an act of kindness that stopped you, a recovery, a forgiveness, a moment in prayer, something beautiful. Not something you read, but something you saw or heard, with its details coming back. If you pray, give thanks for it and hold the line, we cannot but speak; if you don't, just hold the memory.
Parrēsia. The Greek word for the boldness of two unlettered fishermen before the council, the courage that came from having been with Jesus. Today's word.

539.title: Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5:1–11)
539.hook: a hard story about lying to the community
539.carry: the bible keeps the hard stories
539.howItsDone: Catholics examine their conscience, often at night, and confess serious sins in the sacrament of penance; the early community's sharing in Acts 4 and 5 is read at Mass in the Easter season.

segments.voice: Yesterday, parrēsia: two unlettered, ordinary men, bold before the council. Your line was they had been with Jesus.

Founding stories tend to get polished. The brochure keeps the triumphs and quietly drops the rest. So this part of Acts surprises. Luke has just described the first Christians in Jerusalem as one heart and one soul, sharing everything, so that no one among them was in need. A man named Barnabas sells a field and lays the money at the apostles' feet. And right after that glowing picture, Luke tells a story that is very hard to read.
screen: `THE STORY LEFT OUT.` → `ONE HEART AND ONE SOUL.` → `THEN, A HARD STORY.`

segments.voice: A married couple, Ananias and Sapphira, sell a piece of land too. They keep back part of the money and bring the rest, presenting it as the whole. Nobody required them to sell, or to give it all. Peter says so: while it remained, was it not yours? And after it was sold, wasn't the money in your power? The problem isn't the amount. It's the pretending. Peter tells Ananias: "Thou hast not lied to men, but to God." And Ananias falls down and dies. About three hours later Sapphira comes in, not knowing what has happened. Peter asks her straight: did you sell the land for so much? She says yes, for so much. And she falls down and dies too. Great fear came upon the whole church, Luke says: in Greek, the ekklēsia, the assembly. What do we do with a story like this? The text doesn't explain how they died, or say anything about their eternal fate. Some readers see God's judgment; others see a shock so great it killed them. The passage itself doesn't settle it. What it does show is that a community built on sharing can be poisoned by pretending, by people performing a generosity they don't have. And Luke didn't leave it out. The Church's founding story includes this, and Peter's denial, and the disciples' squabbles. So ends week seventy-seven: feed my sheep, witness, Matthias, Peter's first sermon, silver and gold, we cannot but speak, and a hard story.
screen: `ONE HEART, THEN A PRETENSE.` · `NOT THE AMOUNT: THE PRETENDING.` · `THE FIRST CHURCH, IN FEAR.` · `LUKE DIDN'T LEAVE IT OUT.` · then, large: `ANANIAS AND SAPPHIRA.`

segments.voice: Let one small pretense come to mind: saying fine when it isn't, a number rounded up, a story improved. No punishment, just honesty; picture setting the record straight, or simply not adding to it. If you pray, bring it to God as it is, or think of it in light of the sacrament of confession; if you don't, just see it clearly.
Ekklēsia. Luke's word for the assembly of believers, seized by fear after Ananias and Sapphira's pretense was exposed. Today's word.
Your line: the bible keeps the hard stories. Tomorrow, a careful voice in the council. Day five hundred thirty-nine, done.
